faq.a: It helps locate the lesion: absent reflexes point to peripheral nerve or muscle disease, while hyper‑reflexia suggests central involvement.
faq.q: Why is a reflex exam crucial?

faq.a: Severe malaria can cause rhabdomyolysis and peripheral neuropathy; treat malaria promptly and monitor CK.
Rely on clinical pattern, CK, nerve‑specific signs and treat presumptively for the most likely cause.
faq.q: What if EMG is not available?

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer with HIV presents with distal numbness and foot drop – what investigations prioritize and why? — Nerve conduction study to differentiate axonal vs demyelinating neuropathy; CD4 count and viral load to assess HIV control.
A patient with fluctuating ptosis improves after rest – which bedside test confirms the diagnosis and what is the next step? — Ice‑pack test; start pyridostigmine and arrange antibody testing.

You suspect Guillain‑Barré in a child with ascending weakness but nerve studies are unavailable – what clinical criteria guide your diagnosis? — Rapid progression, areflexia, and albumin‑cytologic dissociation if lumbar puncture possible.

A malaria patient develops dark urine and muscle pain – what lab test is essential and what complication must you prevent? — Serum CK; monitor renal function and hydrate to prevent acute kidney injury.
Why are aminoglycoside antibiotics avoided in Myasthenia gravis? — They block neuromuscular transmission, worsening weakness.

In a diabetic with foot ulcer, you find reduced ankle reflexes – how does this affect your management? — Indicates peripheral neuropathy; intensify glycaemic control and foot care to prevent ulcer progression.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with hand‑foot syndrome and weakness – which cause is most likely and how do you treat? — Acute vaso‑occlusive muscle ischemia; give analgesia, hydration and transfusion if severe.
What is the significance of a normal CK in a patient with suspected polymyositis? — Early disease may have normal CK; diagnosis relies on clinical pattern, EMG and possibly muscle biopsy.
ai.title: Neuromuscular Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Neuromuscular disorders are diseases that impair the peripheral nerves, neuromuscular junction or muscle, causing weakness, fatigue and functional loss. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern, bedside tests and selective investigations, often limited in low‑resource settings.

b: Identify pattern: proximal vs distal weakness, fatigable vs fixed.
Use bedside tests: power grading, reflexes, sensory exam, fatigability tests.
sections.p: A neuromuscular disorder is any condition that disrupts transmission of impulses from motor neurons to skeletal muscle or the muscle’s ability to contract.

b: MRC 0‑5 scale for each muscle group.
Stage chronic progressive diseases (e.g., ALS) by King's Clinical Staging.
sections.p: Severity is graded by functional impact (e.g., Medical Research Council (MRC) scale) and need for assistive devices.

b: Peripheral neuropathy: diabetes, HIV neuropathy, TB meningitis, malnutrition (vit B1, B12).
Neuromuscular junction: Myasthenia gravis, organophosphate poisoning.
Muscle: Polymyositis, HIV‑associated myopathy, malaria‑related rhabdomyolysis, sickle‑cell myopathy.
sections.p: Causes are grouped by site of lesion and epidemiology; in East Africa infectious and metabolic causes are common.

b: Proximal weakness → myopathy or MG.
Distal sensory loss → peripheral neuropathy.
Fluctuating weakness worsening with use → MG or cholinesterase toxicity.
sections.p: Patients present with weakness that may be symmetric, focal, proximal or distal, often with associated fatigue, cramps or sensory changes.

t.b: Quantifies muscle strength; guides severity and monitoring.
Absent reflexes suggest peripheral neuropathy; hyper‑reflexia points to central involvement.
Distinguishes demyelinating vs axonal neuropathy; detects myopathic patterns.
Elevated in myopathies, rhabdomyolysis; normal in pure neuropathy.
Positive in Myasthenia gravis; if unavailable, rely on clinical fatigability tests.
Detect diabetic neuropathy; treat underlying hyperglycaemia.
Identify infectious contributors common in low‑resource settings.

b: Rapidly progressive weakness → consider Guillain‑Barré or spinal cord compression.
Respiratory muscle involvement → impending respiratory failure.
Severe CK rise >5,000 U/L → rhabdomyolysis with risk of acute kidney injury.
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent action.

b: Infection‑related neuropathy: appropriate antimicrobial (e.g., anti‑TB, antiretroviral).
Myasthenia gravis: pyridostigmine (cholinesterase inhibitor) and steroids; avoid aminoglycosides.
Inflammatory myopathy: high‑dose steroids first line; steroid‑sparing agents if needed.
Supportive: physiotherapy, orthotics, respiratory physiotherapy, monitor electrolytes.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide symptomatic support and prevent complications.

b: Re‑assess MRC score every 3‑6 months.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce infection‑triggered exacerbations.
Educate on avoiding neurotoxins (e.g., organophosphates).
sections.p: Regular functional assessment and monitoring for drug toxicity or disease progression.

b: Stroke – focal weakness with upper‑motor‑neuron signs.
Spinal cord compression – level‑specific sensory loss and hyperreflexia.
Electrolyte imbalance (hypokalaemia) – generalized weakness but rapid correction improves.
Normal CK does not exclude early neuropathy.
Seronegative Myasthenia gravis – antibodies may be absent; rely on clinical tests.
EMG may be normal in early inflammatory myopathy.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening weakness, especially facial or respiratory muscles.
Severe myoglobinuria with dark urine indicating rhabdomyolysis.
